slots.practicalActivity: Pick one report, spreadsheet, or dashboard number you check regularly (work or personal -- a bank balance or fitness app total is fine). Without opening any system, write down every hop you believe that number passes through from its origin to your screen, then note which of the four business reasons lineage matters (trust, impact analysis, root cause analysis, audit/regulatory) would actually apply if that number turned out to be wrong. Finally, write your hop list twice: once as business lineage (plain system and domain names only) and once as technical lineage (as specific as you can get -- table names, column names, or at least specific tool names).
slots.deliverable: A written hop list for one real number, produced in both business-lineage and technical-lineage form, plus a note on which of the four reasons lineage matters would apply to it.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the same report or number from the previous slot, pick one column feeding it and trace, by hand, exactly which downstream column(s) it actually feeds -- noticing how much more work column-level tracing takes than drawing one table-level arrow. Then decide which of the three lineage-capture approaches (manual documentation, static parsing, runtime capture) would actually be feasible for that pipeline, and justify your choice in one sentence.
slots.deliverable: A column-level trace for one real column, plus a one-sentence justification for which lineage-capture approach fits that pipeline.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice: pick a second report or number, different from the previous two slots, and produce a complete Chapter 1 analysis for it in one pass -- the hop list, the business-lineage version, the technical-lineage version, a column-level trace for one key field, and the capture approach you'd use for it -- without referring back to the lesson videos.
slots.deliverable: A one-page lineage brief for a new report, covering its hops, both lineage views, one column-level trace, and a justified capture approach.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick one real pipeline you know, at work or on a personal project. Identify its source-system category (OLTP database, SaaS/API, or file/stream) and its extraction method (full, incremental, CDC, or API pull). Then decide whether it's ETL or ELT by checking whether raw, untransformed data ever lands anywhere you can query it.
slots.deliverable: A one-paragraph classification of one real pipeline: source category, extraction method, and ETL vs. ELT, with the reasoning behind each choice.

lessons.title: Lineage Through Data Lakes and Warehouses

slots.practicalActivity: Sketch a bronze/silver/gold medallion layering for the pipeline you classified in the previous slot, even if it doesn't formally use that terminology today. Then pick one measure you've seen in any report (a Total Revenue, a Conversion Rate) and sketch its lineage as a chain showing which warehouse column(s) feed it, and whether the semantic model it lives in would be Import or DirectQuery.
slots.deliverable: A bronze/silver/gold sketch for one real pipeline, plus a measure-lineage chain for one real report measure with Import/DirectQuery noted.

slots.practicalActivity: If you have access to a Power BI workspace with Contributor role or higher, open its Lineage view and select one artifact's double-arrow icon, noting how many artifacts light up versus dim -- a rough measure of its blast radius. If you don't have access, sketch what you'd expect your own team's primary report's chain to look like instead. Then write down your best guess at one dashboard's full source-to-screen chain before checking it against the real lineage view or Microsoft Purview, if available.
slots.deliverable: A documented blast-radius count (real or sketched) for one artifact, plus a full source-to-dashboard chain guess for one real dashboard, with any gap from the real lineage noted.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab: trace one real end-to-end pipeline you know, start to finish, writing out every hop from source system through extraction, transformation (ETL or ELT), lake/warehouse layer, semantic model, and final report or dashboard -- labeling each hop with the specific Chapter 2 concept it demonstrates (source type, ETL vs. ELT, medallion layer, Import vs. DirectQuery, or the Power BI lineage view).
slots.deliverable: One complete, hop-by-hop lineage trace for a real pipeline, with every hop labeled by the Chapter 2 concept it illustrates.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the chain you traced in the previous slot's lab, list everything directly upstream of its final report (one hop back) and anything else downstream of the same underlying table, flagging which items you're confident about versus guessing at. Then find one calculated field in that chain and write down, in plain English, every business rule you can identify buried inside its formula or logic.
slots.deliverable: An upstream/downstream list for one real chain with confidence noted, plus a plain-English breakdown of the business rules inside one calculated field.

slots.practicalActivity: Using the dependency chain from the previous slot, pick one field and imagine renaming or removing it. Walk downstream as far as you can, listing every consumer you find and flagging any that would qualify as a Critical Data Element under the criteria from the Metadata Management course. Then reformat that same analysis as a short change impact assessment: what's changing, who's affected, a high/medium/low risk level with a one-sentence justification, and a rollback plan.
slots.deliverable: A downstream impact-analysis list with CDEs flagged, reformatted into a complete change impact assessment document.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick a real or hypothetical "this number looks wrong" scenario from your own work or coursework. Walk upstream through as many hops as you can identify, noting for each hop whether the data was already correct entering it or not, until you find the divergence point -- the same process used on the revenue-dashboard example in this lesson.
slots.deliverable: A documented upstream walk for one real or hypothetical wrong number, ending in a clearly identified divergence point.

slots.practicalActivity: Write a short lineage documentation entry for the chain you've been working with: list each node with a one-line description, each edge with its transformation if known, and an owner for each node (a real role, or "unknown -- needs research" if you genuinely don't know). Then sketch that same chain as an actual diagram -- boxes for datasets, arrows for direction, at least one arrow label for a transformation -- once in full detail and once simplified for an executive audience.
slots.deliverable: A nodes/edges/ownership documentation entry plus two diagram sketches (detailed and executive-simplified) of the same chain.

slots.practicalActivity: For the same pipeline, list every hop you believe is fully automatable (code a tool could scan) versus every hop that would require manual documentation (an export, an email, an undocumented step). Then pick one named lineage tool from this lesson (Microsoft Purview, Collibra, Alation, Apache Atlas, or dbt's own lineage graph), visit its official documentation, and find one real example of its lineage graph, comparing it to this course's diagram conventions.
slots.deliverable: An automatable-vs-manual hop list for one real pipeline, plus notes comparing one real tool's lineage graph to this course's diagram conventions.

slots.practicalActivity: For the lineage documentation you built two slots ago, write a short maintenance plan: how often you'd re-check it, what would trigger an update outside that schedule, and who (a role, not a name) should own keeping it accurate -- directly answering the three ordinary decay reasons this lesson names (schema changes, new pipelines, decommissioned systems).
slots.deliverable: A written maintenance plan for one real lineage document, naming a review cadence, update triggers, and an owning role.

lessons.title: Lineage Case Study: A Revenue Report
Lineage Case Study: Customer Data Across Systems

slots.practicalActivity: Using the five-hop Brightleaf Outfitters revenue chain from the first case study, draw your own version on paper (five boxes, four arrows), mark the actual root-cause hop, and circle which other reports were silently affected by the same bug. Then, for the Caldwell & Finch customer case, list three systems in your own work or a personal project that each independently track some version of "the same thing," and identify whether they currently share a deliberate matching key or just an informal one.
slots.deliverable: A hand-drawn root-cause diagram for the revenue case study, plus a 3-system matching-key assessment grounded in your own work.

slots.practicalActivity: Complete the Northfield Pantry practice lab in full: draw the table-level and column-level lineage for its four tables, run the impact analysis for the proposed SalePrice rename and currency-conversion change, and diagnose the $0 Midwest-region root cause. Then run that completed exercise through the full course review checklist, noting which checklist items it would have failed before the fix.
slots.deliverable: A completed Northfield Pantry lab (lineage diagram, impact analysis, root-cause diagnosis) plus a filled-out review-checklist pass noting pre-fix failures.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After finishing this course, a student can trace a real number from its source system through every transformation to the report that displays it, perform impact analysis before a change ships and root-cause analysis after something breaks, and produce lineage documentation and diagrams a teammate could actually follow.
